name: Ellen Pea
approach: M&M Wall, also known as Supercave Wall for the tennis-court-sized cave crossing the cliff at mid-height, is one of the largest roadside walls at Washington Pass. Park at a pullout near milepost 166 on SR-20, about 3 miles east of the hairpin turns (and a similar distance from the Washington Pass summit). From the highway, head directly uphill (north) toward the talus at the base of the Supercave gully, following it up and briefly left before rejoining the gully; it takes roughly 1 hour to reach the lower ledge and about 1 hour 10 minutes to reach the upper ledge and base of the longer routes.

approach_variants.name: Supercave gully to the upper ledge
approach_variants.notes: Park at the roadside pullout near milepost 166 and start straight uphill to the north — there is no trail and no sign. Head for the talus at the foot of the gully that splits the wall; the gully forces you briefly out to the left before you rejoin it higher. Two ledge systems break the wall. The lower one comes first; keep going past it to the upper ledge, where the long routes start. The wall faces due south and there is no shade below the cave, so on a hot day the approach is the hottest part of the route.
approach_variants.season: Late June to September, once the gully has melted out and the lower pitches have dried; the highway over the pass is gated shut all winter, so there is no cold-season access at all.
hazards: Loose talus and creek-bed footing in the approach gully, with rockfall from anyone above you in it
Full south-facing sun on the whole approach with no shade until the cave
Water and seepage on the lower pitches persists into early summer in wet years
The highway is gated closed through winter and well into spring, so the approach can be unreachable by car
approach_variants.baseFinding: Get onto the upper of the wall's two ledge systems — not the first ledge you meet coming up the gully. Then walk right. This is the right-hand line on the wall and the huge cave that gives the wall its name is directly above you, not off to one side. The check on the ground is the first pitch itself: a left-facing corner about forty metres long that runs to a stance directly beneath a pair of twin cracks slanting left. Count the corner's length and look for the twin cracks above the first stance — that pair is unique on this section of wall. Negative markers: if the corner above you is short, slabby and only about twenty-five metres to its anchor, you have drifted left into the middle of the wall and are under the eleven-pitch line; if you are standing on a treed ledge that two separate lines leave from, you are further left again. And if the cave is high above you but you are on a narrow ledge with one lone bolt at ground level, you never left the lower ledge and are on the three-pitch apron route.

waypoints.name: SR-20 pullout near milepost 166 (Washington Pass)
waypoints.note: Park roadside ~3 mi east of the Washington Pass hairpin; ascend talus directly uphill (north) toward the Supercave gully, ~1 hr to the lower ledge.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 to the roadside pullout near milepost 166, about 3 miles east of the hairpin turns and a similar distance from the Washington Pass summit. Park at the pullout itself — this is one of the largest roadside walls at Washington Pass, so the parking is the trailhead and there is no spur road to find. From the shoulder the talus and the Supercave gully are directly above you.

waypoints.name: Upper ledge, M&M Wall
waypoints.note: The 'Supercave' route: 7 pitches of 5.11c passing beneath the wall's huge signature cave; regarded as among the state's finest lines.
waypoints.directions: There is no trail. Climb from the highway to the talus at the foot of the gully that splits the wall; the gully forces you briefly out to the left before you rejoin it higher. Pass the first, lower ledge system and keep going to the upper ledge, where the long routes start, about an hour and 10 minutes from the car.

waypoints.name: M&M Wall (Supercave) base area
waypoints.directions: Walk right along the upper ledge, a treed third-class ledge slanting up and right out of the gully, to its far end with the big cave directly overhead. The first pitch is the left-facing corner about 40 m long that ends below a pair of left-slanting twin cracks.
